This page covers the manual configuration steps required in OpenWebUI after the initial deployment:

1. **Authentication** — wiring Keycloak SSO.
2. **Connections** — adding the direct LLM endpoint and the CRISalid Agents chat API.
3. **Model configuration** — setting up each agent model for the CRISalid AI use case.

---

## Authentication — Keycloak SSO

By default, OpenWebUI ships with local account creation disabled (`ENABLE_SIGNUP=false`). Keycloak acts as a single OIDC endpoint that can broker any identity provider — institutional CAS SSO, SAML2 federation (e.g. Renater), ORCID, or any other — without requiring a separate OpenWebUI password.

Keycloak SSO is not only a convenience here: the access token obtained at login is what OpenWebUI forwards to the CRISalid Agents chat API with every chat request (see [Connections](#connections) below). Without SSO, the agents are not reachable.

### Keycloak client setup

The realm template of the stack (`docker/keycloak/config/crisalid-inst.json.template`, rendered by `docker/configure_keycloak.sh`) already declares what OpenWebUI needs:

- a confidential client **`open-webui`** (standard flow only) with the redirect URIs `${OPENWEBUI_URL}/oauth/oidc/callback` and `http://localhost:8080/oauth/oidc/callback`, and `${OPENWEBUI_URL}` as web origin; its secret is `OPENWEBUI_KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET` in `docker/openwebui/.env`;
- the client scope **`crisalid-agents-audience`** (an *Audience* mapper adding `crisalid-agents` to the access token), attached as a **default** scope of `open-webui`: the chat API only accepts tokens carrying this audience;
- an **access token lifespan of 15 minutes** on the client (`access.token.lifespan` = 900), longer than the realm default, so that OpenWebUI's refresh-ahead window (5 minutes) does not trigger a refresh on every request.

On a realm imported from the template, nothing has to be created by hand. On an existing realm, create the client and attach the scope in the admin console: the steps and the way to verify the resulting tokens are in the [Security → Keycloak → Clients & scopes](../security/keycloak/clients-scopes.qmd) page.

::: {.callout-note}
The [OpenWebUI Keycloak SSO guide](https://docs.openwebui.com/features/authentication-access/auth/sso/keycloak/) provides step-by-step screenshots for the Keycloak side of this setup.
:::

### Environment variables

The shared `docker/.env` holds the public URL of the instance, used to render the realm (redirect URI, web origin):

```env
OPENWEBUI_URL=https://<openwebui-public-host>
```

Then set the following variables in `docker/openwebui/.env`:

```env
# Secret of the open-webui Keycloak client (also rendered into the realm by configure_keycloak.sh)
OPENWEBUI_KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET=<client-secret>
# Allow new users to be created on first SSO login
OPENWEBUI_ENABLE_OAUTH_SIGNUP=true

# Label shown on the SSO login button
OPENWEBUI_OAUTH_PROVIDER_NAME=Institutional login

# Key encrypting the OAuth tokens kept in the server-side sessions (openssl rand -hex 32)
OPENWEBUI_OAUTH_SESSION_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY=<64 hex characters>
```

The client ID (`open-webui`), the OIDC discovery URL and the callback URL have defaults derived from the shared `.env`: the discovery document is `${KEYCLOAK_SCHEME}://${KEYCLOAK_HOST}:${KEYCLOAK_PORT}/realms/${KEYCLOAK_REALM}/.well-known/openid-configuration` — the **public** Keycloak URL, which is the only issuer of the stack — and the callback is `${OPENWEBUI_URL}/oauth/oidc/callback`. `OPENWEBUI_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `OPENWEBUI_OPENID_PROVIDER_URL` and `OPENWEBUI_OPENID_REDIRECT_URI` override them when the realm lives on another Keycloak instance.

Inside the Docker network the public Keycloak hostname resolves to the Keycloak container through a network alias (see [Docker Compose](docker-compose.qmd#keycloak-issuer)); on a local workstation with the TLS profile, OpenWebUI must trust the mkcert certificate authority (see [Local TLS](../dev/local-tls.qmd)).

::: {.callout-warning}
## `ENABLE_SIGNUP` and SSO

`ENABLE_SIGNUP=false` blocks **local** account creation but does **not** prevent SSO-based registration. The `OPENWEBUI_ENABLE_OAUTH_SIGNUP` variable controls whether new accounts can be created on first SSO login. Keep `ENABLE_SIGNUP=false` and set `OPENWEBUI_ENABLE_OAUTH_SIGNUP=true` to allow SSO users while blocking direct sign-ups.
:::

### Upgrading to 0.13

The stack pins `ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:0.13.0-slim`. Two settings of `docker/openwebui/openwebui.yaml` matter when upgrading an instance deployed with an earlier release:

- `ENABLE_OAUTH_ID_TOKEN_COOKIE=false`: the ID token is no longer stored in a browser cookie; the OAuth tokens (access and refresh tokens) live in the server-side session, where OpenWebUI refreshes them ahead of expiry and from where the *System OAuth* connections read the access token.
- `OAUTH_SESSION_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (`OPENWEBUI_OAUTH_SESSION_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in `docker/openwebui/.env`): the key encrypting those tokens at rest. Generate it once with `openssl rand -hex 32`; without it OpenWebUI falls back to `WEBUI_SECRET_KEY`. Changing the key invalidates the current SSO sessions (users sign in again).

Existing users have to sign in again after the upgrade so that a server-side OAuth session, with an access token, exists for them.

### Restart

After editing `.env`, restart OpenWebUI:

```bash
docker compose --profile openwebui up -d openwebui
```

The login page will now show an SSO button alongside (or instead of) the password form.

## Connections

All model connections are configured in **Admin panel → Settings → Connections**.

### Direct LLM connection

Add a direct OpenAI-compatible connection to your LLM provider (e.g. [ILaaS](https://www.ilaas.fr/rag-ilaas/)):

- **URL**: your LLM API base URL (e.g. `https://llm.ilaas.fr/v1`)
- **API key**: your LLM provider API key

::: {.callout-important}
## Keep all models private

After adding the connection, go to **Admin panel → Settings → Models** and set every model to **private** (visible to admins only). Direct LLM models should not be available to end users — they bypass CRISalid Agents entirely and have no access to the knowledge graph.
:::

This connection is used by OpenWebUI's built-in UI features only (see [User interface config](#user-interface-config) below).

### CRISalid Agents connection

Add a second OpenAI-compatible connection for the chat API of the agents:

- **URL**: `http://crisalid-agents-chat-api:9100/v1`
- **Auth type**: **System OAuth**
- **API key**: none
- **Forward cookies**: off

With *System OAuth*, OpenWebUI sends the signed-in user's Keycloak access token as `Authorization: Bearer` with every request to this connection. The chat API validates it (issuer, audience `crisalid-agents`, expiry) and exchanges it for a toolbox token, so that the graph queries run under the identity of the person asking — see [Security](security.qmd#the-agent-layer-crisalid-agents-chat-api). There is no shared key to configure on either side.

`GET /v1/models` lists the agents the `open-webui` client is allowed to call (`AGENT_ALLOW_LIST` in `docker/crisalid-agents/.env`); each one appears as a model.

::: {.callout-note}
The chat API is only reachable inside the Docker network (`agents-network`, `crisalid-front`) — not exposed on the host. The URL `http://crisalid-agents-chat-api:9100/v1` is only valid from within the OpenWebUI container. Requests without a valid token are answered `401`, including the connection test of a wrongly configured auth type.
:::

## User interface config

OpenWebUI uses a dedicated model for built-in UI tasks (chat title generation, follow-up question suggestions, etc.). This must be set to a **private** direct LLM model, not an agent.

Go to **Admin panel → Settings → Interface** and configure:

- **Task model** (or equivalent): select one of the private direct LLM models added above.

This separates UI housekeeping from the CRISalid agent calls, and avoids charging agent calls for background UI tasks.

---

## Agent model configuration

Each CRISalid agent exposed by the chat API appears as a model in OpenWebUI. Each one must be configured to disable capabilities that are irrelevant or incompatible with the agent workflow.

For each agent model, go to **Admin panel → Models**, open the model, and apply the settings below.

### Disable all capabilities

Under **Capabilities**, disable everything:

- Vision
- File Upload
- Web Search
- Image Generation
- Code Interpreter
- Terminal
- Usage
- Citations
- Status Updates
- Builtin Tools

The agent already handles tool calls internally — these OpenWebUI-level capabilities are redundant and may interfere.

### No system prompt

Leave the **System prompt** field empty. CRISalid Agents already defines its own system prompt; adding one here would override or conflict with it.

### Disable evaluations

In **Admin panel → Settings → Evaluations**, disable **Arena Models** to prevent agent models from appearing in the comparison arena.

---

## Global feature flags

In **Admin panel → Settings**, also disable the following globally:

- **Code execution**
- **Image generation**
- **Web search**

These features do not apply to the CRISalid AI use case and add unnecessary surface area.
